content:
It was originally estimated that about 2,145 trees would be felled.

The current project is being undertaken by a joint venture comprising China State Construction Hong Kong, AlMing Construction and China State Construction Civil Engineering. According to a 2024 Legislative Council document, there are approximately 2,270 trees within the project scope, and about 2,145 are expected to be felled, including 10 'trees of special value'—the Aquilaria sinensis (土沉香) and two Ormosia henryi (茸莢紅豆). The authorities plan to replant around 2,140 trees after completion, including Koelreuteria bipinnata (複羽葉欒樹), Magnolia grandiflora (荷花玉蘭) and champaca (黃蘭), among other species.

Without shade from large trees, residents say hot weather feels even more sweltering

Our reporter recently inspected the areas from Marina Cove to Sai Kung town centre and found that trees had been removed along several road sections, including Pak Wai, Marina Cove, Hebe Haven, Pak Kong and the section leading to Sai Kung town centre. Felling was particularly noticeable around Pak Kong: with land levelling underway, the reporter observed that roughly one-third of the trees on the hillside had been cut down; along the road beside Tai Chung Hau Village, at least 15 consecutive trees had also been felled. Some village residents said that with the roadside shade diminishing, the hot weather felt even more oppressive.

Land levelling is in progress on the Pak Kong hillside, and trees on the slope have been felled.

A hole was bored into one of the felled large trees, and a bottle of orange juice was placed inside.

About 1,900 trees unavoidably need to be removed

In response to an enquiry from集誌社, the Highways Department stated that, because the relevant works run very close to densely vegetated slopes on both sides of the road, some trees—particularly those situated on the slopes—had to be removed or transplanted to free up sufficient space for the works. After investigation, it remained unavoidable that around 1,900 trees needed to be removed.

13 Aquilaria sinensis trees, 11 expected to be felled

The authorities said there are 13 Aquilaria sinensis trees within the works area; of these, 11 were assessed—in terms of their form, structure and growing location—as unsuitable for transplantation and had to be removed, while the remaining two would be retained in situ. One Ormosia henryi was also assessed as unsuitable for transplantation and likewise had to be removed; a camphor tree originally slated for transplantation was, after assessment, also required to be removed. Three Indian Banyan trees are being retained in situ.

The authorities said the project team will plant approximately 2,000 trees at suitable locations within the Sai Kung district, such as roadside amenity strips, to enhance the landscape along the road and improve the Sai Kung community environment.

Aquilaria sinensis is classified as Vulnerable

Aquilaria sinensis (土沉香) is a native Hong Kong tree species, mainly distributed in Sai Kung, the north-eastern New Territories and on Lantau Island. As of 2021, there were about 5,000 mature Aquilaria sinensis trees in the territory. The species is classified as rare and is listed as a protected plant under the Protection of Endangered Species of Animals and Plants Ordinance and as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Because its resin can be processed into the precious fragrance 'agarwood', in earlier years—particularly in the Sai Kung area—mainland 'tree-cutting gangs' came to Hong Kong to fell them illegally and sell them on the black market for over HK$10,000.

As for Ormosia henryi (茸莅紅豆), it is an evergreen tree of the legume family (subfamily Papilionoideae, genus Ormosia) and is listed by the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department as a rare and precious plant. The species was first discovered in Happy Valley in 1850 and is now classified as endangered within mainland China.

Regina, a resident of Pak Wai Village, bought a village house some years ago. A self-described 'plant fanatic', her decision to buy the property was entirely due to an old tree standing in front of the house, which she likens to discovering a 'treasure'. Upon learning of the tree-felling in the neighbourhood, she said excitedly: 'It's 2,000 trees, not 200!' She pointed out that Sai Kung has long been known as 'Hong Kong's back garden' and questioned: 'Without those 2,000 trees, can Sai Kung still be called Hong Kong's back garden?'

Regina, a self-described 'plant fanatic', originally decided to buy a house in Sai Kung entirely because of the old tree in front of the property, which she describes as akin to finding a 'treasure'. (Photo provided by Regina)

She said trees are living things that may take a hundred years to grow; once lost, they cannot easily be restored—including the precious Aquilaria sinensis. Taking Pak Wai Village as an example, she noted that visitors may not remember the village's name, but they do remember the old tree at the village entrance, which has even become a bus stop landmark. 'The reason I can see the mountain is because of these trees—try removing them, and how am I supposed to see the mountain?' She believes the government should not take a one-size-fits-all approach that sacrifices nature conservation.

Neighbours feel a deep attachment to the old trees

Amy, another Sai Kung resident, said that three generations of her family, including her children, have grown up in Sai Kung. 'Seeing the trees gone, it's as if all those years of growing up here are gone too.' Without her glasses on, she joked that her eyesight had been excellent all these years thanks to being surrounded by greenery, with lush woods visible in the distance. 'Suddenly they cut them down, and even the children will end up needing glasses.'

Beyond witnessing the disappearance of the trees, she lamented the many changes Sai Kung has undergone over the years. For example, several historic buildings out along the Sai Kung highway—including the 1946-established China Paint factory, famous for its 'Chrysanthemum', 'Giraffe' and 'Toy' brands—are set to be demolished and redeveloped into residential properties. She also pointed out that, when an old tree in town was toppled by a recent super typhoon, neighbours flocked to 'check in' at the scene—a sign, she said, of how attached residents are to the old trees.

The highway has become 'patchy and unsightly' along the way

Sai Kung resident Mr Tam said that, although he did not know the exact number of trees felled, it was obvious that the trees along the route had diminished. 'There used to be so many trees and it was very pleasant; now you see it all patchy and broken up, and it feels uncomfortable.' He noted that when he moved to Sai Kung one to two years ago, large-scale tree felling had not yet begun, and he also felt it was a pity that the Aquilaria sinensis were being cut down. He questioned whether widening the road would help ease congestion, pointing out that going into Sai Kung on a public holiday is 'expected to be jammed anyway'.

An 84-year-old Sai Kung resident, 'Uncle', has lived in the district for more than 20 years. He said that, with over a thousand trees having been felled, the Sai Kung landscape had become unrecognisable, and he questioned: 'What's traffic congestion got to do with those trees? Your cars don't drive through the trees, do they?'

Cheung-yuet Wong, director of Friends of the Earth, said that when project consultants assess trees, it is perhaps not deliberate, but to facilitate construction it is easy for them to end up 'picking holes', resorting to a 'chop it down if it can't be transplanted' approach rather than trying to save each tree one by one. For example, trees of common species almost have to be 'perfect' to be retained; some trees, even in fair condition, are listed with negative factors if they have minor flaws or slightly inadequate growing space. Large trees can cost over a million dollars to transplant, or may decline as a result of procedures or the difficulty of finding a suitable location.

In principle, Aquilaria sinensis should be preserved as far as possible

He acknowledged that some locations in Sai Kung are on slopes, making the digging of root balls and transplantation more difficult, but if conservation is the goal, options such as significantly pruning the canopy or reducing the size of the root ball should be considered, with 'preserving the species' and 'keeping the tree alive' as the primary aims. With the population of Aquilaria sinensis having dropped sharply, the principle should be to preserve them as far as possible. He also worried that, as additional traffic lanes and median facilities are added to the road, there will be insufficient space to plant trees along the route, turning what was once a shady stretch into vast expanses of concrete, which could in the long run affect the experience of waiting for buses and walking along the road.
